Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Gambia rely entirely on paper-based recording for criminal cases and complaints. Official manuals mandate use of station diaries, pocket diaries, and Diary of Action for logging arrests, statements, incidents, and actions, with no reference to digital tools. Procedures describe manual writing, signing, and copying entries. In March 2026, Inspector General of Police Seedy Mukhtar Touray called for transition from paper documentation to digital systems for speed, cost savings, and efficiency, indicating current nationwide reliance on paper. UNDP-supported community policing includes mobile data apps linked to case management in some areas like Upper River Region, but this is for patrols and reporting, not core station case dockets; represents isolated donor project. No evidence of digital case management rollout at majority of rural stations; new model stations (GIZ/EU-funded) emphasize infrastructure/human rights, not IT. Barriers include lack of training facilities, mobility, rural electricity access (31% per BTI), and infrastructure. National digital ambitions (e.g., NDP digital nation) and justice pilots (UNDP feasibility study for digital case mgmt) exist, but rural point-of-service remains manual, with data likely aggregated upward manually.

revised_comments: Rural police stations in The Gambia record cases and complaints entirely on paper. Officers use station diaries, pocket diaries and the Diary of Action to log arrests, statements, incidents and actions, with no digital tools referenced in official procedural manuals. In March 2026, Inspector General of Police Seedy Mukhtar Touray publicly confirmed that the force still relies on paper-based documentation and called for a transition to a faster, cheaper digitalised mode of records management. A national Automated Fingerprint Identification System launched in April 2026 modernises forensic and criminal-records capacity at Police Headquarters but does not extend digital case recording to rural stations. Isolated donor-supported community policing initiatives use mobile apps for patrol reporting in some areas (e.g. Upper River Region), but these do not cover core case dockets. Barriers include limited rural electricity access, lack of training infrastructure and mobility constraints.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Gambia predominantly use paper registers and structured forms for recording patient data such as antenatal visits, immunizations, and child health. Data is manually aggregated and transcribed into DHIS2 at district or regional levels for national reporting. The Smart Paper Technology (SPT) hybrid system—where paper forms are scanned and digitized post-visit, then synced to DHIS2—has been scaled nationally for the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) and piloted in urban facilities like Bundung Maternal and Child Hospital, enabling mother-child record linkage and improved data quality. However, point-of-care recording remains paper-based even in SPT areas. Limited pilots like TB e-Tracker exist in some rural sites. Key barriers include unreliable electricity, internet connectivity, scanning equipment shortages, and staff training needs, especially in rural areas. While national policy emphasizes HMIS/DHIS2, rural facilities lag with paper as default; digital efforts are donor-driven pilots or aggregation tools, not routine point-of-service use. No evidence majority of rural clinics digitally record data onsite.World Bank PHC Assessment;Nigeria Health Watch SPT

revision_notes: Confirmed, with fresher and more precise evidence. The original sources (World Bank PHC assessment, Nigeria Health Watch, PMC) broadly support 'mostly paper - some digital', but the Smart Paper Technology (SPT) system technically digitises forms at regional scanning centres rather than at the facility, so on a strict facility-level reading SPT alone would not count as digital capture per the metadata guidance. A March 2026 peer-reviewed study (Darboe et al., Union) confirms a genuine facility-level digital pilot: the DHIS2 TB e-Tracker, running at 11 sites (5 of them rural district hospitals - Bansang, Basse, Essau, Farafenni, Soma) since mid-2024, where health workers enter TB case data directly into tablets at the point of care alongside continuing paper registers. This remains a limited pilot rather than majority practice, so 'mostly paper - some digital' is confirmed as the best-supported score.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in The Gambia predominantly record patient data such as antenatal visits, immunisations and child health on paper registers and forms at the point of care. The Smart Paper Technology (SPT) system, used nationally for the Expanded Programme on Immunisation, keeps data capture paper-based at the facility while forms are scanned and digitised at regional centres, so digitisation effectively occurs above facility level. A more advanced pilot, the DHIS2 TB e-Tracker, has since 2024 enabled genuine point-of-care digital data entry via tablets at 11 sites, including several rural district hospitals, run in hybrid with continuing paper registers. Coverage remains limited to these pilot sites. Persistent barriers to wider digital point-of-service capture include unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, shortages of devices, and staff training gaps, particularly in rural areas.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Gambia primarily use manual, paper-based and ledger systems for birth and civil registration, as confirmed in 2020 UN report stating systems for births, deaths, and marriages are not digitized, with only early digitization efforts like pictorial capture under CRVSNOW.UN Gambia CRVS COVID Report Pre-2020, registration was entirely paper-based per World Bank.World Bank Mass Registration Recent eCRVS rollout (2022-23) via health facilities with satellite internet scaled to all facilities, including rural, enabled mass registration of 1.17M people digitally, but focused on health-linked campaigns, not routine point-of-service at dedicated rural registry points.World Bank Mass Registration No evidence majority rural registries routinely use digital at point of care; health facilities may aggregate digitally, but registry remains paper-default with donor digital pilots. Barriers: poor rural internet (addressed via satellite for health), limited infrastructure, low coverage historically (59%). National ambition for eCRVS exists, but rural registry reality lags, relying on paper with upward digital transcription.

revision_notes: Score revised upward from 2 to 3. The original comments and cited sources (World Bank result page, 2020 UN CRVS report, SESRIC presentation) accurately described the 2022-23 position but understated how far routine practice has since moved. Fresh evidence shows the shift from a one-off mass-registration campaign to routine, digital, point-of-service registration: a March 2024 World Bank results note confirms the Ministry of Health 'has transitioned from mass registration to providing routine registration services in all public health facilities' via the eCRVS system, with devices (desktops, laptops, tablets, scanners) distributed to registration centres nationwide and satellite internet extended to all health facilities including rural ones. An April 2026 Ministry of Health statement states the birth and death registration process is now fully digitised, with new QR-coded digital certificates replacing the old paper format nationwide. Marriage registration, however, remains a separate, paper-based process administered by the Ministry of Justice (physical Civil Marriage Form submission), so full 'entirely digital' status is not supported. Because births and deaths make up the great majority of vital events and are now captured digitally at the point of registration, 'mostly digital - some paper' (3) is the best-supported score. This is a substantive but not maximal score change on the scale, so it is not escalated to human review.
revised_comments: Rural civil registration in The Gambia is now mostly digital. Following a World Bank-financed project, the Ministry of Health transitioned from a paper-based, manual system to an electronic Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (eCRVS) system, distributing digital registration devices (desktops, laptops, tablets, scanners) to registration centres nationwide and extending satellite internet to all health facilities, including rural ones. Since 2024 this has moved from a one-off mass-registration campaign to routine, digital point-of-service registration of births and deaths, with new QR-coded digital certificates replacing the former paper format. Marriage and divorce registration remains a separate, paper-based process administered by the Ministry of Justice. As births and deaths represent the large majority of registered vital events, rural civil registration is best characterised as mostly digital with some continuing paper-based elements.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in The Gambia predominantly use paper-based recording for administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. The 2025 Education Statistics Summary Report indicates only 13.2% of schools (10.5% lower basic/primary) have internet for teaching and 15.6% have pedagogical computers nationally, with urban-rural divides exacerbating low access in rural areas (e.g., Regions 5N/6). EMIS data collection relies on school heads' contributions, likely paper forms aggregated centrally. Digital systems like DHIS2 for Education and SEMIS app have been piloted (200 schools in 2020) and scaled nationally by 2021, enabling school-level entry of enrolment, attendance, and performance data via offline Android/Chromebooks, with live dashboards and School Report Cards. However, low infrastructure (electricity 57% in lower basic schools) limits routine point-of-service use in most rural facilities. Key barriers: poor connectivity/electricity, teacher training gaps, multi-grade rural classes. National ambition via MoBSE/GPE KIX/DHIS2 contrasts with rural reality of predominant paper with donor-piloted digital tools.

revision_notes: Confirmed, with fresher corroborating evidence. The original score of 2 is supported. Since 2021 the SEMIS App (built on DHIS2) has enabled individual-level learner data entry via offline Android/Chromebook devices at national scale, and in September 2024 a 'One Laptop Per School' initiative began equipping school managers/administrators with laptops nationwide to support administrative record-keeping, alongside the 2023 GAMREN rollout extending connectivity to schools. However, the October 2025 Education Statistics Summary Report shows only 13.2% of schools (10.5% of lower basic/primary) have internet for teaching, only 15.6% have pedagogical computers, and only 57% of lower basic schools have electricity, confirming that routine point-of-service digital data capture remains the exception rather than the rule in rural primary schools. This keeps the facility-level score at 'mostly paper - some digital' rather than higher.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in The Gambia predominantly record administrative data, attendance and learning outcomes on paper. National policy has pursued digitisation since 2019 through the DHIS2-based SEMIS App, scaled nationally by 2021 for individual learner data entry via offline Android/Chromebook devices, and a 'One Laptop Per School' initiative launched in 2024 to equip school managers with laptops for administrative record-keeping. Nonetheless, the Ministry of Basic and Secondary Education's 2025 Education Statistics Summary Report shows that only 13.2% of schools (10.5% of lower basic/primary schools) have internet access for teaching, only 15.6% have pedagogical computers, and only 57% of lower basic schools have electricity. These infrastructure gaps, concentrated in rural regions, mean that most rural primary schools still rely predominantly on paper-based record-keeping at the point of service, with digital tools used only in a minority of facilities.
